clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant vascular malformation syndrome caused by mutations in RASA1 (CM-AVM type 1) or EPHB4 (type 2)
Characterised by multifocal small, round, pinkish-red capillary malformations, often with a pale halo
A minority of patients harbour fast-flow lesions: arteriovenous malformations or fistulae in skin, muscle, bone or the central nervous system
Parkes Weber syndrome (a limb overgrowth with fast-flow malformations) is part of the RASA1 spectrum
Family history is common given dominant inheritance, though expression is highly variable
Screening for intracranial or spinal arteriovenous lesions is considered because of the risk of haemorrhage
The multiple small capillary malformations distinguish it from a solitary port-wine stain
reference.pathophysiology: RASA1 encodes p120-RasGAP and EPHB4 encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase; both act as negative regulators of RAS-MAPK signalling in vascular endothelium. Loss-of-function mutations, typically with a somatic second hit in individual lesions, dysregulate endothelial proliferation and vessel patterning, producing multifocal capillary malformations and, less often, high-flow arteriovenous malformations or fistulae. The two-hit mechanism accounts for the multifocal, patchy distribution and variable expressivity within families.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination of the skin for multifocal capillary malformations
Genetic testing of RASA1 and EPHB4
Imaging (MRI/MRA) where a fast-flow malformation is suspected
Brain and spine imaging to screen for arteriovenous lesions
Assessment of affected relatives given dominant inheritance
redFlags: Neurological symptoms suggesting an intracranial or spinal arteriovenous malformation
A rapidly enlarging, warm or pulsatile lesion indicating fast flow
Limb overgrowth suggesting Parkes Weber syndrome
reference.prognosis: Most patients have only cutaneous capillary malformations with an excellent prognosis; outcome is worse when high-flow arteriovenous malformations, particularly intracranial ones, are present.
pitfalls: Mistaking multifocal capillary malformations for ordinary port-wine stains
Failing to consider screening for central nervous system arteriovenous malformations
Overlooking the diagnosis in a family with variable, subtle skin findings
Not recognising Parkes Weber syndrome as part of the spectrum
management: Genetic testing of RASA1 and EPHB4 to confirm the diagnosis and guide surveillance
Brain and spine MRI/MRA to screen for intracranial and spinal arteriovenous malformations given the haemorrhage risk
Doppler ultrasound and MRA to identify and characterise fast-flow cutaneous lesions
Embolisation or surgical treatment of symptomatic high-flow arteriovenous malformations by an interventional and vascular team
Pulsed dye laser for cosmetically troublesome capillary malformations
Referral to a vascular anomalies multidisciplinary team, particularly where central nervous system lesions are present
Genetic counselling and cascade screening of relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity
